title: Arrays and Indexed Sequences
learningObjectives: Explain arrays or indexed sequences as ordered collections accessed by position.
Use zero-based index concepts to locate elements in common array systems.
Describe how array length and valid index range are related.
Recognize that fixed-size and dynamic arrays differ by language.
Avoid invalid indexes and test empty, single-element, and boundary cases.

understand.concept: An array or indexed sequence stores elements in an order and allows access using an index or position. In many languages indexes begin at zero, so a sequence of length n has valid indexes from 0 through n - 1. Some arrays have fixed size, while other array-like structures can grow or shrink.
understand.whyItMatters: Indexed access is useful when position matters, such as selecting the first item, reading a row of data, or processing values in order. Boundary mistakes can lead to invalid access or skipped elements.
understand.analogy: A row of numbered lockers gives each position a label. The label identifies a location, not the value stored inside it. The first locker may be numbered 0 in a programming sequence.
understand.analogyLimit: Indexing conventions and array mutability vary. Some languages use one-based indexing, bounds-checking, or fixed-size arrays; the zero-based examples are common but not universal.

explain.narrative: Arrays are useful when the data has a sequence and position matters. Access by index is often direct, but the index must be within the valid range. Use the collection's length and a correct loop condition. Do not confuse an element's value with its index. Arrays may also have language-specific constraints such as fixed size, element type, or storage layout.

examples.title: Use length as the loop boundary
examples.code: for (let i = 0; i < colors.length; i++) { console.log(colors[i]); }
examples.explanation: The loop visits indexes 0 through length - 1, stopping before the invalid index equal to length.

examples.title: Handle an empty sequence
examples.explanation: The length is zero, so there are no valid element indexes and a boundary-aware loop runs zero times.

commonMistakes: Using an index equal to the collection length.
Assuming index 1 means the first item in a zero-based array.
Confusing index values with element values.
Assuming all array structures can grow dynamically.
Skipping boundary tests for empty or one-element arrays.
